title: How One Cancer Cell Escapes and Spreads
narration: A single cancer cell can leave a tumor and start a whole new tumor somewhere else in the body.
So how does cancer spread through a process called metastasis?
First the cell hits the basement membrane, a thin sheet of collagen and other proteins surrounding the tumor.
The cell secretes MMP enzymes, molecular scissors that cut protein.
These enzymes chew the basement membrane into a ragged hole.
The cell crawls through the gap toward a nearby blood vessel.
It slips between vessel-lining cells and enters the bloodstream.
This entry step is called intravasation into circulation.
But blood flow shear forces batter the loose cell hard.
Immune cells and shear stress kill most within a day.
One survivor uses a trick to hide from the immune system.
It grabs platelets, the clotting cells, from the blood.
The platelets clump into a shield masking it from immune attack.
Cloaked, it drifts until flow slows in a tiny vessel.
It lodges in a narrow capillary too small to pass.
It pushes back out through the wall — called extravasation.
It anchors to the new tissue using surface adhesion molecules.
That one cell can divide, seeding a micrometastasis.
A brand-new tumor grows far from its origin.
Here's the strangest part of the story.
The odds against any one cell are staggeringly steep — fewer than one in ten thousand cells succeed.
Only rare cells, some aided by platelet cloaking, slip past the body's defenses.
From that single hidden survivor, a whole second tumor arose.
So the deadliest journey a cell takes is this quiet escape.
